National Register of Historic Places nomination, Otis Elevator Company Building (reference number 99001265), National Park Service.
sources.label: National Register of Historic Places nomination, National Park Service

historical_record.description: The Otis Elevator Company's western assembly plant was built over 1923 and 1924 on a lot 275 by 137.5 feet, designed by the company's own architectural office in Yonkers. It went up as two storeys, the lower one tall enough to take railway wagons, with combed brick and tan terra cotta on the street fronts, eighteen bays along Beach Street and nine along Grant Avenue, each bay carrying one tall round-headed arched window under a Lombard band of six small arches. A railway spur ran in through the Grant Avenue side.

The plant assembled lifts and made the selector mechanism for the company's Signal Control System, and served the whole United States west coast plus Nevada, Arizona, Alaska and Hawaii, with smaller buildings of similar design in Los Angeles and Portland.
With new construction at a standstill through the Depression, the plant was turned over entirely to servicing and maintaining lifts rather than building them.

The lift company left in 1969 and the building became offices for a health insurer. A middle floor was inserted into the tall ground storey, making three floors of two; the internal railway track and sliding crane came out; the lower window sash was replaced with a black metal storefront system and the end-bay windows enlarged to match the rest; and the two Beach Street entrances were closed up in favour of a new recessed entrance in the eighth and ninth bays.

The interior was stripped back for multimedia tenants: the concrete piers exposed, the dropped ceilings taken out with the piping and wiring left showing, and the inserted middle floor removed in two places to restore rooms of the original double height under the skylights.

Listed on the National Register of Historic Places, significant for the part its lifts played in the building boom that changed the San Francisco skyline in the late 1920s, and for the assembly and control manufacture carried on here.

hook: The Otis Elevator Company's west-coast assembly plant of 1924, with a railway spur through the Grant Avenue wall.
